Renato, I have read the form. Before you sit down with him, tell me in your own words how the six months have gone.
Strong, on the whole. He has been covering the interior since January, and his track record on new accounts is the best in the team.
And the ratings? I see a three on planning, and fours everywhere else.

That is right. Two milestones have been reached: the backlog is down from forty accounts to twelve, and the first order from Ribeirao Preto was signed in May. I want to acknowledge both in the meeting.
Good. And is there anything you have been avoiding saying to him?

One thing. The area for improvement is reporting. The weekly report has been arriving after the regional meeting since April. He has not been underperforming on results, but the team cannot plan around a report that does not arrive.
Say it exactly like that. One sentence, and then stop. Most managers say it and then spend a minute taking it back.
Understood. We move to a one-to-one every two weeks, and if it is late twice more I will escalate it to the Director.
That is a real appraisal. And write down that you acknowledged the workload — turnover in the interior has been high for two years, and retention of this one matters.

How long have you been managing this territory?

I have been sitting in performance conversations for eleven years, and most of the bad ones fail in the same place. They fail at the beginning. The manager opens with a soft sentence about the year in general, then a second soft sentence, and by the time the real point arrives the person has stopped listening, because they know something is coming and they are just waiting for it. A good conversation does three things and nothing else. It says what the person has been doing well, with one piece of evidence, not five. It names one area for improvement, once, in plain words, and it does not soften it away in the next sentence. And it ends with something that changes before the next review, agreed out loud by both people. Here is the part managers do not believe. Nobody has ever left a company because a manager was clear. People leave because six months of work was reviewed in four minutes by somebody who had not been paying attention.

I postponed an appraisal for four months. Not because I was busy, although that is what I told myself. I postponed it because the conversation was going to be uncomfortable, and every week it became a little more uncomfortable to have. By the time we sat down, the thing I needed to say was not news any more. It was a habit. He had been arriving late to client meetings since February, and by June the clinics had started to mention it to me instead of to him. What I learned is that the cost of waiting is never paid by the manager. It is paid by the person, who spends four months not knowing something everybody else already knows. I also learned that the same thing happens in reverse with good work. I had been thinking for months that his relationship with the hospitals was the best in the team, and I had never said it out loud. He told me afterwards that he had been considering another offer. One sentence, four months earlier, would have been enough.

Over the last six months you have been carrying the heaviest workload in the territory, and the backlog has come down from forty accounts to twelve. The one area for improvement is the weekly report, which has been arriving late since April. From now on the report goes out every Friday before six. I will hold a one-to-one with you every two weeks instead of every month.
